analysis.one_liner: Removes the federal tax exemption from bonds that finance professional sports stadiums and arenas.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor, hearing, or vote after its October 1999 referral to Ways and Means.
analysis.plain_summary: Cities and counties routinely borrow money for stadiums and arenas through tax-exempt municipal bonds, which means bond buyers pay no federal tax on the interest. That lost tax revenue is a federal subsidy that lowers the cost of building facilities used by billionaire team owners and millionaire athletes. This bill would reclassify bonds that finance professional sports facilities as private-activity bonds, which are taxable and subject to caps, ending that hidden subsidy while grandfathering projects already approved.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who no longer quietly fund stadium construction through foregone tax revenue, and anyone who thinks local governments should compete for teams with their own openly voted money rather than a federal tax break.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reclassifies any bond whose proceeds go directly or indirectly to professional sports facilities as a private activity bond, which loses the tax-exempt status that makes stadium borrowing cheaper [S2][S3].
It closes avoidance through related parties, related facilities, and multiuse complexes by directing the Treasury Secretary to write anti-abuse regulations [S3].
It treats any use of the facility that generates a monetary benefit for a professional sports user as a prohibited use, even when the public or press is admitted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Professional team owners and leagues, who would face higher borrowing costs for stadium projects, and the municipal bond market, which would lose a category of tax-exempt issuance. Cities still hoping to finance a stadium with tax-exempt borrowing would pay more too.
analysis.who_pays_short: Team owners and stadium bond issuers

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers every project with final bond resolutions or official approvals before October 18, 1998, plus current refundings, so nearly all deals in the pipeline would keep their tax exemption [S3].

A good-faith objection: stadiums are built by local governments, and the tax-exempt bond is a general municipal finance tool; removing it raises costs for those cities without stopping subsidies, which may simply shift to other local funding like sales or hotel taxes.
Some argue sports facilities generate construction jobs and local development, so removing the federal subsidy could reduce activity supporters of those projects want [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is ending a quiet federal subsidy to a handful of wealthy sports franchises, worth real revenue to the Treasury over time. The cost falls on team owners and stadium-financing cities through higher borrowing costs, and the grandfather clauses mean the bill would have changed little for deals already underway. The trade is favorable to ordinary taxpayers, though the bill was so narrow and so heavily grandfathered that its practical effect would have been modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and nothing ever happened to it again before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Sanford introduced the bill on October 18, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired with the 106th Congress in January 2001 [S5].
Not a single representative cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Professional sports teams and owners, who kept access to tax-exempt federal subsidies for stadium financing, and the municipal bond market that profits from issuing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Team owners and the municipal bond market

for.name: Rep. Mark Sanford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it received no cosponsors and no committee action.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred under Chairman Bill Archer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until it died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Professional sports leagues and team owners
against.what_they_did: Were the constituency for keeping the tax exemption; the proposal targeted exactly the subsidy they relied on, and no member of either party backed it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors on either side, so the partisan shape of any opposition is unknown.

industries.note: The bill removes their access to tax-exempt municipal bonds, a federal subsidy that lowers the cost of stadiums built largely for their benefit. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against taxpayers.

industries.industry: Municipal bond underwriters and investment banks
industries.note: They earn fees issuing stadium bonds, and taxable private-activity bonds are a smaller, capped market than tax-exempt bonds. The bill would shrink a niche of their business.

Cities would pay higher borrowing costs to attract or keep teams, though they could still finance stadiums with taxable bonds or local taxes. The bill grandfathers projects approved before October 18, 1998.
